title: Factoring Special Products
short: Spot differences of squares and perfect-square trinomials.
trouble: Students factor x² + 9 as (x + 3)(x − 3), not seeing that a sum of squares does not factor over the reals.

blocks.html: The special products work backward too. If you recognize the pattern, you can factor in one step instead of searching for numbers, as you did for general trinomials.

Because $(a + b)(a - b) = a^2 - b^2$, any difference of two squares factors: $x^2 - 49 = (x + 7)(x - 7)$. Because $(a + b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2$, a trinomial whose first and last terms are squares and whose middle term is twice their product is a perfect square. A sum of squares, like $x^2 + 9$, does not factor with real numbers: $x^2 + 9$ is at least $9$ for every real $x$, so it is never $0$, while a factor $(x - r)$ would make it $0$ at $x = r$.

blocks.name: areamodel
blocks.cap: $(x + 7)(x - 7)$: the two middle rectangles, $+7x$ and $-7x$, cancel, leaving $x^2 - 49$.

blocks.html: Look for squares. Square minus square: $(a + b)(a - b)$. Square, twice the product, square: $(a \pm b)^2$. A sum of two squares does not factor over the real numbers.

blocks.title: Perfect square trinomial
steps: Middle check: $2 \cdot 2x \cdot 3 = 12x$, with a minus sign.

blocks.html: Factoring $x^2 + 9$ as $(x + 3)(x - 3)$. Multiply it back: $(x + 3)(x - 3) = x^2 - 9$, the wrong sign. A sum of squares stays as it is; it is already factored completely over the real numbers.
